text: Parents, depths, subtree sizes in one DFS.

7 dep 4, sz 1
A tree with n nodes is connected and has exactly n − 1 edges, so there is exactly one simple path between any two nodes. Pick a root and every node gets a parent, a depth and a subtree.

Store the tree as an undirected adjacency list and pass the parent into the DFS so it never walks back up. One DFS fills fa, dep and sz: sz[u] = 1 + the sizes of its children, added after the child returns.
1: fa 0, dep 1, sz 7 2: fa 1, dep 2, sz 4 3: fa 1, dep 2, sz 2 4: fa 2, dep 3, sz 1 5: fa 2, dep 3, sz 2 6: fa 3, dep 3, sz 1 7: fa 5, dep 4, sz 1

Work done before the children (pre-order) can use the parent's values: depth, distance from the root. Work done after (post-order) can use the children's values: size, sums, the best answer inside the subtree.
Counting nodes within distance d of the root is a depth filter (P5908); counting pairs of edges with a common middle node needs only each node's neighbours (P1351 联合权值).
A path-shaped tree of 10⁵–10⁶ nodes makes the recursion that deep. Usually fine with an enlarged stack (most judges); otherwise use a BFS order and process it backwards.
Two farthest-node searches; the most balanced cut.
The diameter (直径) is the longest path in the tree. With non-negative weights: DFS from any node to the farthest node u; then DFS from u to the farthest node v. The path u–v is a diameter.

Why it works: the farthest node from any start is an end of some diameter. With negative weights this fails; use the DP instead: at each node, longest + second-longest downward path through different children.

Diameter uses: the core of a tree network (P1099 树网的核) lies on a diameter; the "longest round trip" puzzle (P4408) takes the diameter and the best third node; choosing k core cities (P5536) cuts from the middle of a diameter.

Centre of the tree: the middle node(s) of a diameter, minimising the farthest distance. Do not confuse it with the centroid below, which minimises the largest piece. 1 pieces 4, 2 2 pieces 1, 2, 3 3 4 5 6 7

The centroid (重心) is the node whose removal leaves the largest remaining piece as small as possible. Pieces are the children's subtrees and the part "above": n − sz[u]. The largest piece is then at most n / 2.

The centroid also minimises the sum of distances to all nodes (P1395 会议). A tree has one centroid, or two adjacent ones. Repeatedly splitting at centroids gives depth O(log n), the basis of point divide-and-conquer (点分治).

A neighbour v is a child of u exactly when sz[v] < sz[u] (after rooting at 1), so no parent array is needed. The smallest index wins ties because of the strict <. Moving the root from u to a child v changes the distance sum by n − 2·sz[v]: the "rerooting" trick behind P1395 and P2052 道路修建 .
Binary lifting, distances, differences on a tree.
The lowest common ancestor LCA(u, v) is the deepest node that is an ancestor of both. Binary lifting (倍增 , 第3章): up[u][k] = the 2k-th ancestor of u, filled by up[u][k] = up[ up[u][k−1] ] [k−1].
Query: lift the deeper node to the same depth, using the binary digits of the difference. If they meet, done.
Otherwise, for k from high to low, jump both while up[u][k] ≠ up[v][k]; the answer is then up[u][0]. O(log n) per query.

Distance between u and v: dep[u] + dep[v] − 2·dep[LCA]. Do two paths a–b and c–d meet? Yes exactly when the deeper of LCA(a, b) and LCA(c, d) lies on the other path (P3398 仓鼠找 sugar). The fill up[u][k] = up[up[u][k-1]][k-1] works inside the DFS because ancestors are visited first.

Tree differences (树上差分): to add 1 to every node on the path s–t, mark +1 at s and t, −1 at the LCA and −1 at its parent. Afterwards a node's value is the sum of marks in its subtree (P3128). Many paths cost O(1) each, plus one final DFS.
For edges on the path (store each edge at its lower node): +1 at s and t, −2 at the LCA. Used with binary search on the answer in 运输计划(P2680), and per-depth counting in 天天爱跑步(P1600).
Heavy chains + a segment tree over dfn.
1 dfn 1 2 dfn 2 3 dfn 6 4 dfn 5 5 dfn 3 6 dfn 7 7 dfn 4
Heavy-light decomposition (重链剖分): each node's heavy child is the child with the largest subtree. Heavy edges form chains (1-2-5-7, 3-6, 4).
Number the nodes in a DFS that visits the heavy child first: every chain becomes a block of consecutive dfn, and every subtree too.

Going up from any node to the root crosses at most log₂ n light edges, because each light edge at least doubles the subtree size. So any path is O(log n) chain pieces, each a range of dfn: a segment tree over dfn handles path and subtree updates and queries.

Subtree of x = dfn range [dfn[x], dfn[x] + sz[x] − 1]; path x–y = O(log n) chain ranges, so each operation costs O(log² n) (P3384). The same loop finds the LCA: when both are on one chain, the shallower one is the answer.

Edge values: store each edge at its lower endpoint and skip the LCA itself, i.e. the last range is [dfn[x] + 1, dfn[y]] (P3038 Grass Planting). Node colours and "nearest marked ancestor" (P4092, P4116) use the same chains with a different segment tree.
Two easy slips: comparing dep[x] with dep[y] instead of dep[top[x]] with dep[top[y]] in the loop, and forgetting that son[u] = 0 needs sz[0] = 0 for the first comparison.

Key points to memorise
1. Tree: n − 1 edges, one path between any two nodes; DFS with the parent passed in.
2. Pre-order uses the parent (depth); post-order uses the children (size, sums).
3. Diameter (w ≥ 0): farthest from any node = u; farthest from u = v.
4. Centroid: minimise max(n − sz[u], children sizes); largest piece ≤ n / 2.
5. up[u][k] = up[up[u][k−1]][k−1]; lift to equal depth, then jump while different.
6. dist(u, v) = dep[u] + dep[v] − 2·dep[LCA].
7. Path +1 on nodes: s, t +1; LCA, fa[LCA] −1; then subtree sums. Edges: LCA −2.
8. HLD: heavy son first in dfs2; chain = consecutive dfn; subtree = [dfn, dfn + sz − 1].
9. Path loop: move the node whose top is deeper; O(log n) chains per path.
